The model sees `task` by default, since the library adds a `general-purpose` subagent type, and sees the five `*_async_task` tools only when the agent is given at least one async subagent spec (`name`, `description`, `graph_id`, optional `url`) for a remote Agent Protocol server such as LangGraph Platform or a self-hosted server. The Deep Agents Code CLI (`deepagents-code`, also run as `dcode`, forked from `deepagents-cli` at v0.1.0 on 2026-05-12) builds its agent with the library's `create_deep_agent`, so both surfaces share these tools; the CLI reads async subagents from the `[async_subagents]` section of `config.toml` and can ask the user to approve `task`, `start_async_task`, `update_async_task`, and `cancel_async_task` calls. The JS port uses the same tool names; its `task` tool keeps `description` ("The task to execute with the selected agent") and `subagent_type`, while its async tools take camelCase `agentName` (in place of `subagent_type`), `taskId`, and `statusFilter`.

#### `task` (spawn)

Description (verbatim):

```text
Launch an ephemeral subagent to handle a complex, multi-step task.

Available agent types and the tools they have access to:
{available_agents}

Specify subagent_type to select the agent. Usage notes:
- Launch multiple agents concurrently when their tasks are independent, using a single message with multiple tool calls.
- Each invocation is stateless by default: the agent sees only the prompt you give it and returns a single final report. Put full detail in the prompt and state exactly what it should return - unless an agent type below says it inherits your conversation instead.
- The agent's report is not shown to the user; relay a summary yourself.
- Tell the agent whether to create content, analyze, or only research, since it can't necessarily see the user's intent unless it inherits your conversation, as noted per agent type below.
- If an agent's description says to use it proactively, do so without waiting to be asked.
- When only general-purpose is available, use it for any complex, context-heavy task; it has the same capabilities as the main agent.
```

Parameters (Python pydantic model, verbatim):

```python
class TaskToolSchema(BaseModel):
    """Input schema for the `task` tool."""

    description: str = Field(
        description=(
            "A detailed description of the task for the subagent to perform autonomously. "
            "Include all necessary context and specify the expected output format."
        )
    )

    subagent_type: str = Field(description=("The type of subagent to use. Must be one of the available agent types listed in the tool description."))
```

Source (description and parameters): Deep Agents source, `libs/deepagents/deepagents/middleware/subagents.py` lines 403-414 (schema) and 442-453 (`TASK_TOOL_DESCRIPTION`), commit 9f0e39d - source at commit, 2026-10-10; fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog. The class's `_reject_unknown_keys` validator (lines 416-439) follows the fields and is described below. Both fields are required.

Semantics. `task` blocks: it invokes the subagent and returns, as the tool result with no envelope, the subagent's `structured_response` serialized as JSON when one is set, otherwise the text of its last non-empty AI message. `description` holds the full task text, not a short label; since 2026-09-22 (PR #6299) the schema rejects any other key with "Unexpected argument {key!r}; put all instructions for the subagent in `description`.", a change made after issue #6286 reported that Claude Sonnet 5, on deepagents 0.7.13, kept leaving "a short label in `description`" and writing "the actual instructions into an extra key" such as `prompt` (forum or issue, 2026-09-13 and 2026-09-22). `{available_agents}` is filled with one `- {name}: {description}` line per subagent type, an unknown type returns "We cannot invoke subagent {subagent_type} because it does not exist, the only allowed types are {allowed_types}", and a type declared with `mode="fork"` inherits the parent's conversation, has " (inherits your full conversation and system prompt - no need to restate context here)" appended to its line, and gets the `task` tool itself with a recursion guard. A caller can replace the whole description through the `task_description` argument, which may contain `{available_agents}`. `task` has been the tool name since the first commit on 2025-07-29, and the README says the project was "Inspired by Claude Code: an attempt to identify what makes it general-purpose, and push that further." (source at commit, 80338eda64fd and README.md).

#### `start_async_task` (spawn)

Description (verbatim):

```text
Start an async subagent on a remote server. The subagent runs in the background and returns a task ID immediately.

Available async agent types:
{available_agents}

## Usage notes:
1. This tool launches a background task and returns immediately with a task ID. Report the task ID to the user and stop - do NOT immediately check status.
2. Use `check_async_task` only when the user asks for a status update or result.
3. Use `update_async_task` to send new instructions to a running task.
4. Multiple async subagents can run concurrently - launch several and let them run in the background.
5. The subagent runs on a remote server, so it has its own tools and capabilities.
```

Parameters (Python pydantic model, verbatim):

```python
class StartAsyncTaskSchema(BaseModel):
    """Input schema for the `start_async_task` tool."""

    description: str = Field(description="A detailed description of the task for the async subagent to perform.")
    subagent_type: str = Field(description="The type of async subagent to use. Must be one of the available types listed in the tool description.")
```

Source (description and parameters): Deep Agents source, `libs/deepagents/deepagents/middleware/async_subagents.py` lines 138-142 (schema) and 173-183 (`ASYNC_TASK_TOOL_DESCRIPTION`), commit 9f0e39d - source at commit, 2026-10-10; fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog.

Semantics. The call returns at once with "Launched async subagent. task_id: {task_id}"; the subagent runs as a run on a thread of the remote server, and the task id is that thread id. `{available_agents}` is filled with one `- {name}: {description}` line per async subagent spec, and an unknown type returns "Unknown async subagent type `{agent_type}`. Available types: {allowed}". No completion notice is pushed to the parent and there is no blocking wait tool; the parent reads results with `check_async_task`, and task records are kept in agent state under `async_tasks` so they survive context compaction. The tool was added as `launch_async_subagent` on 2026-03-16 and renamed `start_async_task` on 2026-03-20, when the companion tools' id parameter changed from `job_id` to `task_id` (source at commit, 0c5d501066e7 and 66c526053c7e).

#### `check_async_task` (output, status)

Description (verbatim):

```text
Check the status of an async subagent task. Returns the current status and, if complete, the result. Statuses shown earlier in the conversation are always stale, so call this to get the current status rather than reporting a status from a previous tool result.
```

Parameters (Python pydantic model, verbatim):

```python
class CheckAsyncTaskSchema(BaseModel):
    """Input schema for the `check_async_task` tool."""

    task_id: str = Field(description="The exact task_id string returned by start_async_task. Pass it verbatim.")
```

Source (description and parameters): Deep Agents source, `libs/deepagents/deepagents/middleware/async_subagents.py` lines 145-148 (schema) and 466-470 (description, three concatenated string literals), commit 9f0e39d - source at commit, 2026-10-10; fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog.

Semantics. The result is `json.dumps` of an object with `status` and `thread_id`, plus `result` (the content of the thread's last message, or "(completed with no output messages)") when the status is `success`, or `error` when the status is `error`. An unknown id returns "No tracked task found for task_id: {task_id!r}". Before 2026-03-20 the tool was `check_async_subagent` with a `job_id` parameter (source at commit, 66c526053c7e).

#### `update_async_task` (message)

Description (verbatim):

```text
Send updated instructions to an async subagent. Interrupts the current run and starts a new one on the same thread, so the subagent sees the full conversation history plus your new message. The task_id remains the same.
```

Parameters (Python pydantic model, verbatim):

```python
class UpdateAsyncTaskSchema(BaseModel):
    """Input schema for the `update_async_task` tool."""

    task_id: str = Field(description="The exact task_id string returned by start_async_task. Pass it verbatim.")
    message: str = Field(description="Follow-up instructions or context to send to the subagent.")
```

Source (description and parameters): Deep Agents source, `libs/deepagents/deepagents/middleware/async_subagents.py` lines 151-155 (schema) and 570-574 (description, three concatenated string literals), commit 9f0e39d - source at commit, 2026-10-10; fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog.

Semantics. The result is "Updated async subagent. task_id: {task_id}", and the task id does not change, because the new run starts on the same thread. Before 2026-03-20 the tool was `update_async_subagent` (source at commit, 66c526053c7e).

#### `list_async_tasks` (list)

Description (verbatim):

```text
List tracked async subagent tasks with their current live statuses. By default shows all tasks. Use `status_filter` to narrow by status (e.g. 'running', 'success', 'error', 'cancelled'). Use `check_async_task` to get the full result of a specific completed task. Statuses shown earlier in the conversation are always stale, so call this to read current statuses rather than reporting one from a previous tool result.
```

Parameters (Python pydantic model, verbatim):

```python
class ListAsyncTasksSchema(BaseModel):
    """Input schema for the `list_async_tasks` tool."""

    status_filter: Literal["running", "success", "error", "cancelled", "all"] | None = Field(
        default=None,
        description="Filter tasks by status. One of: 'running', 'success', 'error', 'cancelled', 'all'. Defaults to 'all'.",
    )
```

Source (description and parameters): Deep Agents source, `libs/deepagents/deepagents/middleware/async_subagents.py` lines 164-170 (schema) and 802-809 (description, six concatenated string literals), commit 9f0e39d - source at commit, 2026-10-10; fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog.

Semantics. The tool fetches each tracked task's live status from its server and returns "{n} tracked task(s):\n" followed by one line per task in the form `- task_id: {task['task_id']}  agent: {task['agent_name']}  status: {status}`. Before 2026-03-20 the tool was `list_async_subagent_jobs` (source at commit, 66c526053c7e).

#### `cancel_async_task` (cancel)

Description (verbatim):

```text
Cancel a running async subagent task. Use this to stop a task that is no longer needed.
```

Parameters (Python pydantic model, verbatim):

```python
class CancelAsyncTaskSchema(BaseModel):
    """Input schema for the `cancel_async_task` tool."""

    task_id: str = Field(description="The exact task_id string returned by start_async_task. Pass it verbatim.")
```

Source (description and parameters): Deep Agents source, `libs/deepagents/deepagents/middleware/async_subagents.py` lines 158-161 (schema) and 653 (description), commit 9f0e39d - source at commit, 2026-10-10; fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog.

Semantics. The result is "Cancelled async subagent task: {task_id}", or "Failed to cancel run: {e}" when the server call fails. Before 2026-03-20 the tool was `cancel_async_subagent` (source at commit, 66c526053c7e).

### LangGraph Supervisor

- Openness: open source, MIT license
- Version described: langgraph-supervisor-py commit `88859b34017ac3569bbd4a3092c7e77593a0a960` (2026-07-14)
- Target models: not stated in the sources; `create_supervisor` takes any LangChain `LanguageModelLike`, and its docstring example uses `gpt-4o`
- Sources:
  - langgraph-supervisor-py source, `langgraph_supervisor/handoff.py`, https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph-supervisor-py/blob/88859b34017ac3569bbd4a3092c7e77593a0a960/langgraph_supervisor/handoff.py - source at commit, 2026-07-14
  - langgraph-supervisor-py source, `langgraph_supervisor/supervisor.py`, https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph-supervisor-py/blob/88859b34017ac3569bbd4a3092c7e77593a0a960/langgraph_supervisor/supervisor.py - source at commit, 2026-07-14
  - langgraph-supervisor-py README, https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph-supervisor-py/blob/88859b34017ac3569bbd4a3092c7e77593a0a960/README.md - source at commit, 2026-07-14
  - GitHub repository metadata for langchain-ai/langgraph-supervisor-py, https://api.github.com/repos/langchain-ai/langgraph-supervisor-py - first-hand, fetched 2026-10-10

`create_supervisor` builds a supervisor agent that sees one `transfer_to_<agent_name>` handoff tool per managed agent, and the developer can add an opt-in `forward_message` tool. The README opens with "**Note**: We now recommend using the **supervisor pattern directly via tools** rather than this library for most use cases." (README line 3).

#### `transfer_to_<agent_name>` (handoff)

Description (verbatim):

```text
Ask agent '{agent_name}' for help
```

Parameters (Python function signature from source at commit 88859b3, verbatim):

```python
    @tool(name, description=description)
    def handoff_to_agent(
        state: Annotated[dict, InjectedState],
        tool_call_id: Annotated[str, InjectedToolCallId],
    ) -> Command:
```

Source (description and parameters): langgraph-supervisor-py source, `langgraph_supervisor/handoff.py` lines 82-92, commit `88859b3` - source at commit, 2026-07-14; fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog. The description is the f-string default `f"Ask agent '{agent_name}' for help"`, where `{agent_name}` is the agent's name as given; both parameters are injected by LangGraph (`InjectedState`, `InjectedToolCallId`), so the model supplies no arguments.

Semantics. The name is `transfer_to_` plus the agent name trimmed, with whitespace runs replaced by `_`, and lowercased (`_normalize_agent_name`, handoff.py lines 16-18); `create_supervisor` generates one such tool per managed agent unless the developer supplies custom handoff tools for all of them, and `handoff_tool_prefix` swaps the `transfer_to_` prefix (supervisor.py lines 164-186, 331-335), while the README shows a custom tool named `assign_to_math_expert` with description "Assign task to math expert" (README line 200). The tool returns `Command(goto=agent_name, graph=Command.PARENT, ...)`, which moves control to the worker node with the full message history plus a tool message "Successfully transferred to {agent_name}" (handoff.py lines 93-126), so the worker's answer does not come back as this tool's result. Instead each worker node has a graph edge back to the supervisor (supervisor.py lines 457-467), and the worker's messages are appended to the shared history per `output_mode` (default `"last_message"`, or `"full_history"`), followed by a synthesized AI message "Transferring back to {supervisor_name}" that calls `transfer_back_to_<supervisor_name>` with empty arguments and a tool message "Successfully transferred back to {supervisor_name}" (handoff.py lines 132-152, supervisor.py lines 77-99); `transfer_back_to_<supervisor_name>` is never bound to a model as a tool and exists only in those synthesized messages. Parallel handoffs are off by default (`parallel_tool_calls: bool = False`, documented as "only OpenAI and Anthropic") and use `Send` when enabled (supervisor.py lines 222, 310-320; handoff.py lines 100-115), and the library has no status, wait, or cancel tool.

#### `forward_message` (output)

Description (verbatim):

```text
Forwards the latest message from the specified agent to the user without any changes. Use this to preserve information fidelity, avoid misinterpretation of questions or responses, and save time.
```

Parameters (Python function signature from source at commit 88859b3, verbatim):

```python
    @tool(tool_name, description=desc)
    def forward_message(
        from_agent: str,
        state: Annotated[dict, InjectedState],
    ) -> str | Command:
```

Source (description and parameters): langgraph-supervisor-py source, `langgraph_supervisor/handoff.py` lines 155-178, commit `88859b3` - source at commit, 2026-07-14; fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog. The description is three adjacent string literals, shown joined; `state` is injected, so the model supplies only `from_agent`.

Semantics. The tool is opt-in: the developer builds it with `create_forward_message_tool("supervisor")` and passes it in `tools`, and the README says the tool "expects an argument `from_agent` specifying which agent's last message should be forwarded directly to the output" (README lines 274-292). It finds the latest AI message whose name matches `from_agent` (case-insensitive), skipping the synthesized handoff-back messages, copies its content into a new AI message named after the supervisor, and returns a `Command` with `goto="__end__"` (handoff.py lines 179-211). If no message matches, the tool result is "Could not find message from source agent {from_agent}. Found names: {found_names}" (handoff.py lines 189-195).

### LangGraph Swarm

- Openness: open source, MIT license
- Version described: langgraph-swarm-py commit `5442a15cdd0ed210589148900c9960c24c489d04` (2026-09-19)
- Target models: not stated in the sources; the README example uses `ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o")`
- Sources:
  - langgraph-swarm-py source, `langgraph_swarm/handoff.py`, https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph-swarm-py/blob/5442a15cdd0ed210589148900c9960c24c489d04/langgraph_swarm/handoff.py - source at commit, 2026-09-19
  - langgraph-swarm-py README, https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph-swarm-py/blob/5442a15cdd0ed210589148900c9960c24c489d04/README.md - source at commit, 2026-09-19
  - GitHub repository metadata for langchain-ai/langgraph-swarm-py, https://api.github.com/repos/langchain-ai/langgraph-swarm-py - first-hand, fetched 2026-10-10

Each agent in a swarm sees the handoff tools the developer adds to its `tools` list with `create_handoff_tool(agent_name=..., description=...)`, and `create_swarm` takes the agents plus a `default_active_agent` (README lines 41-70).

#### `transfer_to_<agent_name>` (handoff)

Description (verbatim):

```text
Ask agent '{agent_name}' for help
```

Parameters (Python function signature from source at commit 5442a15, verbatim):

```python
    @tool(name, description=description)
    def handoff_to_agent(
        # Annotation is typed as Any instead of StateLike. StateLike
        # trigger validation issues from Pydantic / langchain_core interaction.
        # https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain/issues/32067
        state: Annotated[Any, InjectedState],
        tool_call_id: Annotated[str, InjectedToolCallId],
    ) -> Command:
```

Source (description and parameters): langgraph-swarm-py source, `langgraph_swarm/handoff.py` lines 67-80, commit `5442a15` - source at commit, 2026-09-19; fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog. The description is the f-string default `f"Ask agent '{agent_name}' for help"`, where `{agent_name}` is the agent's name as given; both parameters are injected by LangGraph (`InjectedState`, `InjectedToolCallId`), so the model supplies no arguments.

Semantics. The name is `transfer_to_` plus the agent name trimmed, with whitespace runs replaced by `_`, and lowercased (`_normalize_agent_name`, handoff.py lines 38-40, 67-68), and the README example overrides the description, for example "Transfer to Bob" and "Transfer to Alice, she can help with math" (README lines 45-60). The tool returns `Command(goto=agent_name, graph=Command.PARENT, update=...)`, which appends a tool message "Successfully transferred to {agent_name}" to the full message history and sets `"active_agent": agent_name` (handoff.py lines 81-93), so control moves to the target agent and nothing comes back to the caller as a tool result. The README says "The system remembers which agent was last active, ensuring that on subsequent interactions, the conversation resumes with that agent." (README line 3). The library has no status, wait, or cancel tool.

  - Letta Code commit `dd3a3fbdcb09` (`run_in_background` defaults to true), https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/commit/dd3a3fbdcb09 - source at commit, 2026-07-01
  - Letta Code commit `f61414acebd4` (removes `run_in_background`; always background), https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/commit/f61414acebd4 - source at commit, 2026-08-31
  - Letta Code commit `41d925ace533` ("fix(tools): remove retired task output pollers (#4622)"), https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/commit/41d925ace533 - source at commit, 2026-09-22
  - Letta Code commit `5e0eb86d4c05` (last change to `Task.json` before the pinned commit), https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/commit/5e0eb86d4c05 - source at commit, 2026-10-08

The model sees four subagent tools: `Agent`, `Workflow`, `SendAgentMessage`, and `TaskStop`. All three built-in toolsets (`letta`, `default` labeled "Claude toolset", and `codex`) list `Task` (shown as `Agent`), `SendAgentMessage`, `TaskStop`, and `Workflow` (`src/tools/toolset-catalog.ts`, source at commit). The `TaskCreate`, `TaskGet`, `TaskList`, and `TaskUpdate` tools in the `default` toolset manage a session checklist ("Create a new task in the session task list.", `src/tools/descriptions/TaskCreate.md`, source at commit) and do not manage subagents.

#### `Agent` (spawn)

Description (verbatim):

````text
# Agent

Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks autonomously.

The Agent tool launches specialized subagents that autonomously handle complex tasks. Each subagent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

When launching a new subagent, you must specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. When deploying an existing agent with agent_id or conversation_id, it is optional and defaults to general-purpose.

## When NOT to use the Agent tool:

- To send input to an agent that is already working, use SendAgentMessage when available (Cloud backend). It sends to the existing conversation without waiting for an answer or creating another local task. On the local backend, or for other ways to message an agent, load the messaging-agents skill.
- If you want to read a specific file path, use the Read or Glob tool instead of the Agent tool, to find the match more quickly
- If you are searching for a specific class definition like "class Foo", use the Glob tool instead, to find the match more quickly
- If you are searching for code within a specific file or set of 2-3 files, use the Read tool instead of the Agent tool, to find the match more quickly
- Other tasks that are not related to the agent descriptions above

## Usage notes:

- Always include a short description (3-5 words) summarizing what the agent will do
- Launch multiple agents concurrently whenever possible, to maximize performance; to do that, use a single message with multiple tool uses
- When the agent is done, it will return a single message back to you along with its conversation ID. The result returned by the agent is not visible to the user. To show the user the result, you should send a text message back to the user with a concise summary of the result.
- Agents always run in the background. The tool result includes a task ID and an output_file path, and you will be notified automatically via a <task-notification> message when it completes, so there is no need to poll. The output file receives the report when the agent finishes; it has no interim progress. You can continue working while agents run.
- Agents can be resumed using the `conversation_id` parameter by passing the conversation ID from a previous invocation. When resumed, the agent continues with its full previous context preserved.
- Provide clear, detailed prompts so the agent can work autonomously and return exactly the information you need.
- Agents with "access to current context" can see the full conversation history before the tool call. When using these agents, you can write concise prompts that reference earlier context (e.g., "investigate the error discussed above") instead of repeating information. The agent will receive all prior messages and understand the context.
- The agent's outputs should generally be trusted
- Clearly tell the agent whether you expect it to write code or just to do research (search, file reads, web fetches, etc.), since it is not aware of the user's intent
- If the agent description mentions that it should be used proactively, then you should try your best to use it without the user having to ask for it first. Use your judgement.
- If the user specifies that they want you to run agents "in parallel", you MUST send a single message with multiple Agent tool use content blocks. For example, if you need to launch multiple agents in parallel, send a single message with multiple Agent tool calls.

## External Coding Agents

Use `subagent_type: "claude-code"` or `subagent_type: "codex"` to start a coding worker through the corresponding locally installed CLI. These types use the same background task lifecycle and completion notifications as Letta subagents, but they do not create Letta agents or conversations. Do not combine them with `agent_id` or `conversation_id`. External coding workers always run on the current machine and do not accept the remote-machine option.

The initial receipt includes a synthetic `claude_...` or `codex_...` agent ID as soon as the native session starts. Pass that ID to `SendAgentMessage` to steer active work or start one tracked follow-up turn when idle.

Fresh Letta subagents automatically discover and call the parent's MCP servers through `letta mcp`. This includes local and cloud-attached servers without copying connections or credentials. Deploying an existing agent keeps that agent's MCP scope.

Claude Code and Codex automatically receive the parent's MCP discovery metadata and use the same `letta mcp` CLI through their shell. To advertise a subset:

```typescript
Agent({
  subagent_type: "claude-code",
  description: "Inspect Linear issue",
  prompt: "Read the issue and trace the relevant implementation.",
  mcp: {
    inherit: true,
    servers: ["linear"],
  },
})
```

Omitting `mcp` advertises every MCP server currently available to the parent. `mcp: { inherit: false }` omits the discovery reminder. Adding `servers` advertises exactly that named subset and fails before launch if a requested server is unavailable. These options control discovery, not authorization or a security allowlist.

## Deploying an Existing Agent

Instead of spawning a fresh subagent from a template, you can deploy an existing agent to work in your local codebase.

### Access Levels (subagent_type)

When deploying an existing agent, only `general-purpose` is supported: full read-write access (Bash, Edit, Write, etc.) for implementation and research tasks. If `subagent_type` is not specified, it defaults to `"general-purpose"`.

### Parameters

- **agent_id**: The ID of an existing agent to deploy (e.g., "agent-abc123")
  - Starts a new conversation with that agent
  - The agent keeps its own system prompt and memory
  - Tool access is controlled by subagent_type

- **conversation_id**: Resume from an existing conversation (e.g., "conv-xyz789")
  - Normal `conv-...` IDs are globally unique and do not require `agent_id`
  - If a prior invocation returns the conversation ID `default`, pass both that invocation's `agent_id` and `conversation_id: "default"`; `default` is agent-scoped and cannot identify an agent by itself
  - Continues from the conversation's existing message history
  - Use this to continue context from:
    - A prior Agent tool invocation that returned a conversation_id
    - A message thread started via the messaging-agents skill

### Examples

```typescript
// Deploy an existing agent
Agent({
  agent_id: "agent-abc123",
  subagent_type: "general-purpose",
  description: "Fix auth bug",
  prompt: "Fix the bug in auth.ts"
})

// Continue an existing conversation
Agent({
  conversation_id: "conv-xyz789",
  description: "Continue implementation",
  prompt: "Now implement the fix we discussed"
})

// Continue an agent's default conversation
Agent({
  agent_id: "agent-abc123",
  conversation_id: "default",
  description: "Continue implementation",
  prompt: "Now implement the fix we discussed"
})
```

## Example usage:

```typescript
// Good - specific and actionable
Agent({
  subagent_type: "general-purpose",
  description: "Find authentication code",
  prompt: "Search for all authentication-related code in src/. List file paths and the main auth approach used."
})

// Good - complex multi-step task
Agent({
  subagent_type: "general-purpose",
  description: "Add input validation",
  prompt: "Add email and password validation to the user registration form. Check existing validation patterns first, then implement consistent validation."
})

// Parallel execution - launch both at once in a single message
Agent({ subagent_type: "general-purpose", description: "Find frontend components", prompt: "..." })
Agent({ subagent_type: "general-purpose", description: "Find backend APIs", prompt: "..." })

// Bad - too simple, use Read tool instead
Agent({
  subagent_type: "general-purpose",
  prompt: "Read src/index.ts"
})
```

## Forking Parent Context

Use `subagent_type: "fork"` to launch a subagent that inherits the parent's full conversation history. The subagent runs against a forked copy of the current conversation, so it has all accumulated context without the parent needing to serialize it into the prompt.

This is useful when:
- The subagent needs deep context that would be expensive to re-explain in the prompt
- You want to leverage prompt caching across multiple parallel forked subagents
- The task requires understanding decisions and discussion from earlier in the conversation

```typescript
// Fork with full parent context
Agent({
  subagent_type: "fork",
  description: "Implement auth module",
  prompt: "Implement the auth module we discussed. Use the patterns from the existing code."
})

// Parallel forks share the same cached prefix
Agent({ subagent_type: "fork", description: "Implement component A", prompt: "..." })
Agent({ subagent_type: "fork", description: "Implement component B", prompt: "..." })
```

Note: `fork` cannot be combined with `agent_id` or `conversation_id`.

## Running on Another Computer

Pass `computer` to run the subagent's turn on another connected computer instead of this machine. Prefer a stable device ID or computer name; these select the freshest online listener for that device. Ephemeral connection IDs are still supported to pin a specific listener. Memory workers must run on the current machine; do not set `computer` for `subagent_type: "memory"`. The call fails fast if the named device is offline, the name matches multiple online devices, or the listener is too old to support routing.

`computer: "cloud"` provisions a Cloud sandbox for the subagent's conversation and runs the turn there. Sandboxes are per-conversation: this is a separate machine from wherever you are running now, even if you are already in a Cloud sandbox.

Omit `computer` to run the subagent on the current machine. That is the default and the right choice for almost all tasks - the subagent shares your working directory and files. Only set `computer` when the task specifically needs another machine (its files, its OS, or an isolated sandbox).

```typescript
// Fork this conversation and run the work on a connected computer
Agent({
  subagent_type: "fork",
  computer: "office-mac",
  description: "Run integration tests",
  prompt: "Run the integration suite in the checkout on this machine and report failures."
})

// Deploy an existing agent into a fresh Cloud sandbox
Agent({
  agent_id: "agent-abc123",
  computer: "cloud",
  description: "Build release artifacts",
  prompt: "Build and upload the release artifacts."
})
```

Behavior notes:
- The remote turn runs with the remote machine's working directory, tools, and skills. Subagent-type tool restrictions (e.g. recall's read-only toolset) travel with the turn on current servers; older servers ignore them.
- The remote turn's final assistant message is returned as the task result. Token and step statistics are not available for remote runs.
- Computer-routed tasks are submitted asynchronously and tracked through Cloud's existing Super Run status feed. Temporary status-read failures retry in the background; there is no one-hour tracking ceiling. Completion still notifies you if the reply could not be collected; use `letta messages list` to read the conversation rather than launching the task again. Stopping a task cancels its queued input or its executing listener run.

## Concurrency and Safety:

- **Safe**: Multiple read-only agents (e.g. recall) running in parallel
- **Safe**: Multiple agents editing different files in parallel
- **Risky**: Multiple agents editing the same file (conflict detection will handle it, but may lose changes)
- **Best practice**: Partition work by file or directory boundaries for parallel execution
````

Source: Letta Code source, `src/tools/schemas/Task.json` (last changed in commit `5e0eb86d4c05`, 2026-10-08), commit `271f119d` - source at commit, 2026-10-10 (fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog).

Semantics. Every `Agent` call runs in the background, and the tool result is the receipt "Task running in background with task ID: ${result.task_id}${agentIdLine}${conversationIdLine}\nOutput file: ${result.output_file}\n\nYou will be notified automatically when this task completes - a <task-notification> message will be delivered with the result. No need to poll, sleep-wait, or check the output file. Just continue with your current work." (`src/tools/impl/task.ts`, source at commit). Completion arrives as a `<task-notification>` block holding `<task-id>`, `<status>` (`completed` or `failed`), `<summary>`, `<result>`, and an optional `<usage>` block with `total_tokens`, `tool_uses`, and `duration_ms`, followed by "Full transcript available at: ${notification.outputFile}" when an output file exists (`src/utils/task-notifications.ts`, source at commit); the message role used to inject it is not in the sources. The schema had `run_in_background`, defaulting to true from 2026-07-01 (commit `dd3a3fbdcb09`), until commit `f61414acebd4` removed it on 2026-08-31 and made every run background; until then `required` also included `subagent_type` (source at commit). The polling tool `TaskOutput {task_id, block, timeout}` (timeout in ms, max 600000) was removed on 2026-09-22 in commit `41d925ace533` "fix(tools): remove retired task output pollers (#4622)", together with `BashOutput` and `KillBash` (source at commit). The internal name stays `Task`: `src/tools/tool-name-mapping.ts` maps `Task: "Agent"` under the comment "Align subagent-spawning tool with Claude Code: surface internal `Task` as `Agent`.", a change made on 2026-04-24 in commit `238af7dfb87c` "refactor(tools): surface Task tool as Agent for Claude Code parity (#1911)" (source at commit).

#### `Workflow` (spawn)

Description (verbatim):

```text
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

Workflows run in the background: this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> carrying the script's return value arrives when the workflow completes. Do not poll or sleep for it, and never fabricate the result before it arrives. TaskStop aborts the run.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration - they asked for a workflow or multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "fan out agents"), or invoked a skill whose instructions call this tool. Workflows can spawn many subagents and cost real money. For any other task, even one that would benefit from parallelism, describe what a workflow could do and ask first.

Scripts can also call the agent's MCP tools directly with `await tools.mcp__server__tool(args)`, subject to the user's permission rules.

Scripts are plain JavaScript and must begin with `export const meta = {...}`, a pure literal (no variables, calls, or interpolation). Pass the work list via `args`. Prefer `pipeline()` so each item moves to its next stage as soon as it is ready. Await `agent()` calls: failures reject with the cause, `callIndex`, and `conversationId` when available. `parallel()` and `pipeline()` let siblings finish, then reject if any callback failed; a failed pipeline item skips its remaining stages. Catch errors explicitly inside callbacks for best-effort processing.

  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-files',
    description: 'Review each file for bugs, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const findings = {type: 'object', properties: {bugs: {type: 'array', items: {type: 'string'}}}, required: ['bugs']}
  const verdict = {type: 'object', properties: {real: {type: 'boolean'}}, required: ['real']}
  const results = await pipeline(
    args.files,
    f => agent(`Review ${f} for bugs.`, { phase: 'Review', schema: findings }),
    (review, f) => parallel(review.bugs.map(bug => () =>
      agent(`Is this a real bug in ${f}? ${bug}`, { phase: 'Verify', schema: verdict })
        .then(v => v.real ? { file: f, bug } : null))),
  )
  return results.flat().filter(Boolean)

Before authoring a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill - the script API, pipeline-vs-barrier rules, quality patterns, worked examples, and how to diagnose a run.
```

Source: Letta Code source, `src/tools/descriptions/Workflow.md`, commit `271f119d` - source at commit, 2026-10-10 (fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog).

```json
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "script": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "Self-contained workflow script (plain JavaScript, not TypeScript) starting with `export const meta = {...}`."
    },
    "scriptPath": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "Path to a workflow script file on disk. Takes precedence over `script`."
    },

      "description": "Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string."

      "minimum": 1,

    }
```

Semantics. `Workflow` runs a JavaScript script in the background, and the script launches each subagent with an `agent()` call; the description says the tool "returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> carrying the script's return value arrives when the workflow completes". `maxConcurrent` caps subagents running at once (default 16), and further `agent()` calls queue. `TaskStop` aborts a workflow run. The schema has no required property; `scriptPath` takes precedence over `script`. The description limits use to cases where the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration.

#### `SendAgentMessage` (message)

Description (verbatim):

```text
# SendAgentMessage

Send a message without waiting for its answer. Letta-to-Letta messages require
the Cloud backend and fail on the local backend (`agent-local-` IDs). Use this
to coordinate with an agent already working, including an Agent child, or to
contact any conversation you are authorized to access.

Claude Code and Codex workers return synthetic `claude_...` and `codex_...`
agent IDs backed by their native sessions. A message to active work steers its
in-flight turn (Claude interrupts through stream-json and sends the replacement
instruction; Codex uses app-server turn/steer). An idle follow-up starts one tracked local background
turn. Neither path uses the Cloud messaging backend.

An agent has a persistent identity and shared memory. It can have multiple
conversations, each with its own message history.

- Supply `conversation_id` to message an existing thread, or `agent_id` alone to
  start a new hidden thread with that agent. To use an agent's default conversation,
  supply its `agent_id` and `conversation_id: "default"`. Pass the full
  conversation ID; truncated IDs are rejected.
- Your agent and conversation IDs are attached automatically as the return address.
  To reply, the recipient must explicitly send to that address. Ordinary assistant
  output is not forwarded back to you.
- A successful send means Cloud accepted the message; the recipient may not have
  read it yet. Continue working rather than waiting for the answer.
- Omit `computer` unless a particular computer is needed. If the conversation is
  active on A, selecting B is rejected rather than moving the conversation.
- If delivery cannot be confirmed, check the recipient's messages before resending
  to avoid duplicates. The tool result includes details for inspecting the send.
- Keep sends sparse and useful: concise assignments, specific questions, or
  material updates. Skip status pings and repeated acknowledgments; repeat a
  point only when you have something new to add.
- For work already underway, treat the agent doing it as its owner. Send what it
  needs, then let it decide. Do not take over or redo its work. If you think
  ownership should change, ask the human instead of declaring it in a message.

If you are a subagent, omitting both `agent_id` and `conversation_id` sends to
your parent (the agent and conversation that launched you). Message your parent
rarely: each message stays in both contexts, and your final report already
reaches it. Send one only when a parent decision would otherwise force you to
redo work, stating the default you will take, then keep working. Steering your
own children (Agent, Claude Code, or Codex) is normal; message them as often as
the work needs.

Use Agent to launch or resume a managed Letta child task and receive its
completion notification. Letta-to-Letta sends create no local task ID. External
coding-agent follow-ups may return one when they start a new native turn; an
active external-agent steer remains part of the existing task. SendAgentMessage does not
change the recipient's tools, model, or permissions. Load the messaging-agents
skill for additional CLI options and troubleshooting.
```

Source: Letta Code source, `src/tools/descriptions/SendAgentMessage.md`, commit `271f119d` - source at commit, 2026-10-10 (fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog).

Parameters (JSON Schema from source at commit 271f119d, verbatim):

```json
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "message": {
      "type": "string",
      "minLength": 1,
      "description": "The message to send."
    },
    "agent_id": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "The agent to start a new conversation with. An agent shares its identity and memory across conversations. Omit when targeting an existing conv-... thread; required with conversation_id: default. Claude Code and Codex sessions returned by Agent use claude_... and codex_... IDs; sending to one resumes that native session."
    },
    "conversation_id": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "The existing message thread to send to. Each conversation has its own message history. A conv-... ID is sufficient; to use an agent's default thread, also supply agent_id. A subagent that omits both conversation_id and agent_id messages its parent."
    },
    "computer": {
      "type": ["string", "null"],
      "description": "Optional computer where the recipient should run: cloud, an online computer name, or its stable device ID. Omitted, null, and blank values use its active computer or saved destination (a computer or Cloud sandbox). An offline saved computer does not trigger a Cloud-sandbox fallback."
    }
  },
  "required": ["message"],
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#"
}
```

Source: Letta Code source, `src/tools/schemas/SendAgentMessage.json`, commit `271f119d` - source at commit, 2026-10-10 (fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog).

Semantics. `SendAgentMessage` does not wait for an answer: per its description, "A successful send means Cloud accepted the message; the recipient may not have read it yet." Letta-to-Letta sends require the Cloud backend, fail on the local backend (`agent-local-` IDs), and create no local task ID. For Claude Code and Codex workers started through `Agent`, which return synthetic `claude_...` and `codex_...` agent IDs, a message to active work steers the in-flight turn and a message to an idle worker starts one tracked local background turn. A subagent that omits both `agent_id` and `conversation_id` sends to its parent, and the sender's agent and conversation IDs are attached as the return address.

#### `TaskStop` (cancel)

Description (verbatim):

```text
# TaskStop

- Stops a running background task or monitor by its ID
- Required: `task_id` (the task to terminate; the legacy `shell_id` alias has been removed - bash background shells share the same ID space as other tasks)
- Returns `{ killed: boolean }` indicating whether the task was actively running and got terminated
- Use this tool when you need to terminate a long-running task
```


Source: Letta Code source, `src/tools/schemas/TaskStop.json`, commit `271f119d` - source at commit, 2026-10-10 (fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog).

Semantics. `TaskStop` stops any background task by ID, including `Agent` subagents, `Workflow` runs, monitors, and bash background shells, which share one ID space; it returns `{ killed: boolean }`. For a subagent routed to another computer, the `Agent` description says "Stopping a task cancels its queued input or its executing listener run." Its schema was tightened on 2026-05-14 in commit `2cd273f7a4a7` "refactor(tools): tighten TaskOutput/TaskStop schemas to match Claude Code (#1949)" (source at commit), and the legacy `shell_id` alias has since been removed.

### Letta V1 server

- Openness: open source, Apache-2.0
- Version described: the retired V1 server, read from the `archive` branch at commit `56ba9c25552605eec89de8ed3dc6394b625c1993` (2026-08-13); `main` at commit `5bcdd177d70fa2b31a754cfcd801e77b2e1ab16a` (2026-09-10) is a stub
- Target models: not stated in the sources
- Sources:
  - Letta repository page (license field), https://github.com/letta-ai/letta - first-hand, fetched 2026-10-10
  - Letta `README.md` on `main`, https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/5bcdd177d70fa2b31a754cfcd801e77b2e1ab16a/README.md - source at commit, 5bcdd177 (2026-09-10)
  - Letta `letta/functions/function_sets/multi_agent.py` on `archive`, https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/56ba9c25552605eec89de8ed3dc6394b625c1993/letta/functions/function_sets/multi_agent.py - source at commit, 56ba9c25 (2026-08-13)
  - Letta `letta/constants.py` on `archive`, https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/blob/56ba9c25552605eec89de8ed3dc6394b625c1993/letta/constants.py - source at commit, 56ba9c25 (2026-08-13)

The `main` branch of letta-ai/letta is now a stub whose README says "The current source code lives in [`letta-ai/letta-code`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code)" and "The [`archive`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta/tree/archive) branch contains the retired Letta V1 API server."; the tools below are read from the `archive` branch. The V1 server gives agents three peer-messaging tools, listed in `letta/constants.py` as `MULTI_AGENT_TOOLS = ["send_message_to_agent_and_wait_for_reply", "send_message_to_agents_matching_tags", "send_message_to_agent_async"]`, with `LOCAL_ONLY_MULTI_AGENT_TOOLS = ["send_message_to_agent_async"]`. Each tool is a Python function; the description shown for each is the summary paragraph of its docstring, and the JSON schema the server built from the function is not in the sources.

#### `send_message_to_agent_and_wait_for_reply` (message)

Description (verbatim):

```text
Sends a message to a specific Letta agent within the same organization and waits for a response. The sender's identity is automatically included, so no explicit introduction is needed in the message. This function is designed for two-way communication where a reply is expected.
```

Parameters (Python function signature and docstring, verbatim):

```python
def send_message_to_agent_and_wait_for_reply(message: str, other_agent_id: str) -> str:
    """
    Sends a message to a specific Letta agent within the same organization and waits for a response. The sender's identity is automatically included, so no explicit introduction is needed in the message. This function is designed for two-way communication where a reply is expected.

    Args:
        message (str): The content of the message to be sent to the target agent.
        other_agent_id (str): The unique identifier of the target Letta agent.

    Returns:
        str: The response from the target agent.
    """
```

Source (description and parameters): Letta source, `letta/functions/function_sets/multi_agent.py` on the `archive` branch, commit `56ba9c25` - source at commit, 2026-08-13 (fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog).

Semantics. The call blocks until the target agent answers. The tool reads the sender's ID from the `LETTA_AGENT_ID` environment variable and sends the target a system-role message prefixed "[Incoming message from agent with ID '{sender_agent_id}' - your response will be delivered to the sender]". It returns the string form of `{"agent_id": other_agent_id, "response": assistant_messages}`, where `assistant_messages` lists the target's assistant messages, or `["<no response>"]` if there are none. Agents are addressed by their Letta agent ID; there is no task ID.

#### `send_message_to_agents_matching_tags` (message)

Description (verbatim):

```text
Sends a message to all agents within the same organization that match the specified tag criteria. Agents must possess *all* of the tags in `match_all` and *at least one* of the tags in `match_some` to receive the message.
```

Parameters (Python function signature and docstring, verbatim):

```python
def send_message_to_agents_matching_tags(message: str, match_all: List[str], match_some: List[str]) -> List[dict[str, Any]]:
    """
    Sends a message to all agents within the same organization that match the specified tag criteria. Agents must possess *all* of the tags in `match_all` and *at least one* of the tags in `match_some` to receive the message.

    Args:
        message (str): The content of the message to be sent to each matching agent.
        match_all (List[str]): A list of tags that an agent must possess to receive the message.
        match_some (List[str]): A list of tags where an agent must have at least one to qualify.

    Returns:
        List[str]: A list of responses from the agents that matched the filtering criteria. Each
        response corresponds to a single agent. Agents that do not respond will not have an entry
        in the returned list.
    """
```

Source (description and parameters): Letta source, `letta/functions/function_sets/multi_agent.py` on the `archive` branch, commit `56ba9c25` - source at commit, 2026-08-13 (fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog).

Semantics. The tool selects matching agents other than the sender (with an empty `match_all`, it lists up to 100 agents), then calls `send_message_to_agent_and_wait_for_reply` for each one in turn, so the call blocks until every matched agent has answered. It returns a list of `{"agent_id": ..., "response": [...]}` dictionaries, with `"<error: {exc}>"` as the response for an agent whose send raised an exception, and an empty list when no agent matches.

#### `send_message_to_agent_async` (message)

Description (verbatim):

```text
Sends a message to a specific Letta agent within the same organization. The sender's identity is automatically included, so no explicit introduction is required in the message. This function does not expect a response from the target agent, making it suitable for notifications or one-way communication.
```

Parameters (Python function signature and docstring, verbatim):

```python
def send_message_to_agent_async(message: str, other_agent_id: str) -> str:
    """
    Sends a message to a specific Letta agent within the same organization. The sender's identity is automatically included, so no explicit introduction is required in the message. This function does not expect a response from the target agent, making it suitable for notifications or one-way communication.
    Args:
        message (str): The content of the message to be sent to the target agent.
        other_agent_id (str): The unique identifier of the target Letta agent.
    Returns:
        str: A confirmation message indicating the message was successfully sent.
    """
```

Source (description and parameters): Letta source, `letta/functions/function_sets/multi_agent.py` on the `archive` branch, commit `56ba9c25` - source at commit, 2026-08-13 (fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog).

Semantics. The call is fire-and-forget: it sends the target a system-role message prefixed "[Incoming message from agent with ID '{sender_agent_id}' - this is a one-way notification; if you need to respond, use an agent-to-agent messaging tool if available]" and returns "Successfully sent message", with no ID to wait on or collect. It raises "This tool is not allowed to be run on Letta Cloud." when the server's environment setting is `prod`, and `letta/constants.py` lists it in `LOCAL_ONLY_MULTI_AGENT_TOOLS` (source at commit). The blocking or one-way behavior of the three tools is fixed by the tool name (`_and_wait_for_reply` or `_async`), not by a parameter.

### LlamaIndex AgentWorkflow

- Openness: open source, MIT (`llama-index-core/pyproject.toml`)
- Version described: run-llama/llama_index commit `6dd2f3cdd9ce7ff927ea8d46ccee08875bb00f95` (2026-10-08), `llama-index-core` 0.14.25
- Target models: not stated in the sources
- Sources:
  - LlamaIndex `llama-index-core/llama_index/core/agent/workflow/multi_agent_workflow.py`, https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/6dd2f3cdd9ce7ff927ea8d46ccee08875bb00f95/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/agent/workflow/multi_agent_workflow.py - source at commit, 2026-10-08
  - LlamaIndex `llama-index-core/llama_index/core/agent/workflow/prompts.py`, https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/6dd2f3cdd9ce7ff927ea8d46ccee08875bb00f95/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/agent/workflow/prompts.py - source at commit, 2026-10-08
  - LlamaIndex `llama-index-core/llama_index/core/tools/function_tool.py`, https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/6dd2f3cdd9ce7ff927ea8d46ccee08875bb00f95/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/tools/function_tool.py - source at commit, 2026-10-08
  - LlamaIndex docs `docs/src/content/docs/framework/understanding/agent/multi_agent.md`, https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/6dd2f3cdd9ce7ff927ea8d46ccee08875bb00f95/docs/src/content/docs/framework/understanding/agent/multi_agent.md - source at commit, 2026-10-08

In a multi-agent `AgentWorkflow`, each agent gets one `handoff` tool that lists the agents it may hand off to; a workflow with a single agent, or an agent with no allowed targets, gets no handoff tool (`multi_agent_workflow.py:216-241`). The docs also describe an orchestrator pattern ("Pattern 2 - Orchestrator agent (sub-agents as tools)") in which developers write their own agent-calling tools, with example names `call_research_agent`, `call_write_agent`, and `call_review_agent`; those tools are not built in (`multi_agent.md`).

#### `handoff` (handoff)

Description (verbatim):

```text
Useful for handing off to another agent.
If you are currently not equipped to handle the user's request, or another agent is better suited to handle the request, please hand off to the appropriate agent.

Currently available agents:
{agent_info}
```

Source: LlamaIndex `llama-index-core/llama_index/core/agent/workflow/prompts.py:1-6` (`DEFAULT_HANDOFF_PROMPT`), commit `6dd2f3c` - source at commit, 2026-10-08 (fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog). `{agent_info}` is filled with `str()` of a dict that maps each allowed target agent's name to its description, leaving out the current agent and any agent outside its `can_handoff_to` list (`multi_agent_workflow.py:224-243`); a developer can replace the template through `handoff_prompt`, which must contain `{agent_info}` (`:155-160`).

Parameters (Python function signature and docstring, verbatim; `FunctionTool.from_defaults` builds the schema from the signature and leaves out the `Context` parameter):

```python
async def handoff(ctx: Context, to_agent: str, reason: str) -> str:
    """Handoff control of that chat to the given agent."""
```

Source: LlamaIndex `llama-index-core/llama_index/core/agent/workflow/multi_agent_workflow.py:73-74`, commit `6dd2f3c` - source at commit, 2026-10-08 (fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog), with the `Context` exclusion in `llama-index-core/llama_index/core/tools/function_tool.py:197-255`.

Semantics. The tool is built with `FunctionTool.from_defaults(async_fn=handoff, description=fn_tool_prompt, return_direct=True)`, so the explicit description replaces the function docstring (`multi_agent_workflow.py:243-246`, `function_tool.py:225-231`). A valid call stores `next_agent` and returns "Agent {to_agent} is now handling the request due to the following reason: {reason}.\nPlease continue with the current request." (`prompts.py:15`); an invalid target gets "Agent {to_agent} not found. Please select a valid agent to hand off to. Valid agents: {valid_agents}" or "Agent {to_agent} cannot hand off to {current_agent_name}. Please select a valid agent to hand off to." (`multi_agent_workflow.py:78-85`). Control then moves to the target agent: after the tool step the workflow sets `current_agent_name` to the target, writes the handoff output as an assistant message, and, unlike other `return_direct` tools, does not stop; the next turn runs the target agent on the shared memory, so the target's work does not return to the caller as a tool result (`multi_agent_workflow.py:709-759`). The call has no task id, and there are no status, wait, or cancel tools.

Each sub-agent in an agent's `agents` configuration becomes its own tool named `agent-<agentName>`. When background tasks are enabled, these tools can also run in the background through a per-call `_background` field; there is no model-facing status, wait, or cancel tool. Mastra's agent networks route work through structured output from a routing agent (`{ primitiveId, primitiveType, prompt, selectionReason }`), not through a tool, and the routing prompt says "DO NOT CALL THE PRIMITIVE YOURSELF." (`network/index.ts:704-728`).

#### `agent-<agentName>` (spawn)

Description (verbatim):

```text
agent.getDescription() || `Agent: ${agentName}`
```

Source: Mastra `packages/core/src/agent/agent.ts:5468-5470`, commit `3645c3d` - source at commit, 2026-10-10 (fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog). The description is the sub-agent's own description, or `Agent: <agentName>` when it has none.

Parameters (zod schema in TypeScript source, verbatim):

```ts
const createSubAgentInputSchema = ({ withResultRefs = false }: { withResultRefs?: boolean } = {}) =>
  z.object({
    prompt: z.string().describe('The prompt to send to the agent'),
    ...(withResultRefs
      ? {
          contextFromRefs: z
            .array(
              z.union([
                z.string().min(1),
                z.object({
                  ref: z.string().min(1).describe('Reference ID from a [ref: ...] line'),
                  as: z.string().min(1).nullish().describe('Optional label for this result in the prompt'),
                  note: z.string().nullish().describe('Optional note about why this result is relevant'),
                }),
              ]),
            )
            .nullish()
            .describe(
              'Reference IDs from the [ref: ...] lines of earlier agent results in this task. The full text of each referenced result is inserted before your prompt exactly as it was produced, so you do not need to restate it.',
            ),
        }
      : {}),
    // Using .nullish() instead of .optional() because OpenAI sends null for unfilled optional fields
    threadId: z.string().nullish().describe('Thread ID for conversation continuity for memory messages'),
    resourceId: z.string().nullish().describe('Resource/user identifier for memory messages'),
    instructions: z
      .string()
      .nullish()
      .describe(
        'Additional instructions to append to the agent instructions. Only provide if you have specific guidance beyond what the agent already knows. Leave empty in most cases.',
      ),
    maxSteps: z
      .number()
      .or(z.string().transform(Number))
      .pipe(z.number().int().min(3))
      .nullish()
      .describe('Maximum number of execution steps for the sub-agent (integer, minimum 3)'),
    // using minimum of 3 to ensure if the agent has a tool call, the llm gets executed again after the tool call step, using the tool call result
    // to return a proper llm response
  });
```

Source: Mastra `packages/core/src/agent/agent.ts:292-331`, commit `3645c3d` - source at commit, 2026-10-10 (fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog).

Semantics. The tool name is `agent-${agentName}`, where `agentName` is the key of the sub-agent in the parent's `agents` record (`Object.entries(agents)`, `agent.ts:5447-5469`, `:6551`, `:6568`), and the schema shown is what Mastra generates for every child; `contextFromRefs` is added only when `delegation.enableResultReferences` is on (`:5443-5451`). By default the call runs in the foreground and the model receives `${output.text}` plus any pending sub-agent tool calls and an optional `\n\n[ref: ${output.ref}]` line, unless `delegation.includeSubAgentToolResultsInModelContext` is set, in which case the full output object (`text`, `subAgentThreadId`, `subAgentResourceId`, `subAgentToolResults`) is used (`:333-345`, `:5453-5466`). When background tasks are enabled and the sub-agent has its own background configuration or a background-enabled tool, the agent tool is background-eligible (`:1454-1494`, `:6543-6548`), and the model is told it may pass `"_background": { "disposition": "foreground" | "deferred" | "awaited", "timeoutMs": number, "maxRetries": number }`, where "deferred" means "the tool runs in the background while you continue; you receive a placeholder result with a task ID and are notified when the task completes." (`system-prompt.ts:55-66`). A background call returns `Background task ${verb}. Task ID: ${taskId}. The tool "${toolName}" is running in the background. You will be notified when it completes.` with `verb` one of `started`, `resumed`, `restarted`, `reattached`, or `reconciled` (`background-dispatch-core.ts:160-161`), and on completion Mastra will "replace the "Background task started..." placeholder in the transcript with the real result (or failure)" (`background-task-result-core.ts:20-24`). The output schema reports the sub-agent's thread and resource ids (`subAgentThreadId` "The thread ID of the agent", `subAgentResourceId` "The resource ID of the agent"), and `maxSteps` has a minimum of 3.

The model can see three kinds of subagent tools: one tool per agent wrapped with `agent.as_tool(...)`, one handoff tool per target (`handoff_to_<target_id>`) in the handoff orchestration, and six `background_agents_*` tools from the experimental `BackgroundAgentsProvider` (`@experimental(feature_id=ExperimentalFeature.HARNESS)`), a context provider in the core package's `_harness` module rather than a separately named product. The .NET twin of that provider uses the same six tool names, with different description wording for five of them and C# camelCase parameter names, so each background tool below gives the Python text first and the .NET text after it; .NET handoff and agent-as-tool names are not in the sources. The AutoGen README calls Microsoft Agent Framework "the enterprise-ready successor to AutoGen".

#### `<agent_name>` (spawn)

Description (verbatim, generated):

```text
{agent.description}
```

Parameters (JSON Schema built as a Python dict literal in the source at commit fd52de7, verbatim):

```python

        argument_description = arg_description or f"Task for {tool_name}"
```

Source (description and parameters): Microsoft Agent Framework source at commit fd52de7, `python/packages/core/agent_framework/_agents.py:725-741`; the description is the `description` argument to `as_tool`, else the agent's own description, else an empty string - source at commit, 2026-10-09 (fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog).

Semantics. The tool name is `name or _sanitize_agent_name(self.name)`, where `_sanitize_agent_name` turns every character outside `[a-zA-Z0-9_]` into an underscore, collapses repeated underscores, strips leading and trailing underscores, and returns "agent" if nothing is left (`_agents.py:233-261`); the schema shown is what the framework generates for each wrapped agent, with the argument named `task` (`arg_name: str = "task"`) and described as "Task for {tool_name}" unless `arg_name` or `arg_description` is passed (`_agents.py:657-675`). The call is blocking: the wrapper runs `self.run(str(kwargs.get(arg_name, "")), stream=True, session=session, ...)` and returns `final_response.text` as the tool result (`_agents.py:818-867`). The subagent gets its own private `AgentSession` unless `propagate_session=True`, which gives it a copy of the parent's application state and merges changes back (`_agents.py:678-684`, `:750-816`, `:868-875`). If the subagent asks for tool approval, the call fails with "Agent tool {tool_name!r} cannot continue because its sub-agent requested approval for ..." (`_agents.py:846-863`); `approval_mode` defaults to "never_require".

```csharp
                    [Description("The name of the background agent to delegate the task to.")] string agentName,
                    [Description("The request to pass to the background agent.")] string input,
                    [Description("A description of the task used to identify the task later.")] string description) =>
```

Source (description and parameters): Microsoft Agent Framework source at commit fd52de7, `dotnet/src/Microsoft.Agents.AI/Harness/BackgroundAgents/BackgroundAgentsProvider.cs:612-616` and `:662-667` - source at commit, 2026-10-09 (fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog).

Semantics. The call does not block: it creates a new session for the named agent, starts `bg_agent.run(input, session=sub_session)` as an asyncio task, and returns "Background task {task_id} started on agent '{agent_name}'." (`_background_agents.py:487-512`). Task ids are integers that start at 1 in each session and go up by one per task (`_background_agents.py:194`, `:488`, `:500`); agent names match case-insensitively, and an unknown name returns "Error: No background agent found with name '{agent_name}'. Available agents: {available}" (`:482-485`). The provider injects instructions that say "Creating a background task does not block, and background tasks run concurrently." and "Important: Always wait for outstanding tasks to finish before you finish processing.", followed by a list headed "Available background agents:" with one "- {name}: {description}" line per agent (`_background_agents.py:32-44`, `:179-187`). The provider was added on 2026-05-27 in PR #6069 (forum or issue, merged 2026-05-27).

#### `handoff_to_<target_id>` (handoff)

Description (verbatim):

```text
Handoff to the {target_id} agent.
```

Parameters (Python function from source at commit fd52de7, verbatim):

```python
        @tool(name=tool_name, description=doc, approval_mode="never_require")
        def _handoff_tool() -> None:
            """This function will be intercepted by the auto-handoff middleware thus the body will never execute."""
            pass
```

Source (description and parameters): Microsoft Agent Framework source at commit fd52de7, `python/packages/orchestrations/agent_framework_orchestrations/_handoff.py:392-407`; the description is the default `f"Handoff to the {target_id} agent."`, replaced by the `description` of the `HandoffConfiguration` when one is set (`:93-112`) - source at commit, 2026-10-09 (fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog).

Semantics. The name is `f"handoff_to_{_INVALID_TOOL_NAME_CHARACTERS.sub('_', target_id)}"[:_MAX_TOOL_NAME_LENGTH]`, which turns characters outside `[a-zA-Z0-9_-]` into underscores, keeps case, and cuts the result to 64 characters (`_handoff.py:126-136`); a collision with an existing tool name raises `ValueError` (`:376-383`). The tool takes no arguments: `_AutoHandoffMiddleware` intercepts the call before the function body runs, answers it with the synthetic result `{"handoff_to": target_id}`, and ends the caller's run with `MiddlewareTermination` (`_handoff.py:142-169`). The workflow then adds the handoff to the conversation, routes it to the target agent, and emits a `handoff_sent` event (`_handoff.py:454-475`), so control moves to the other agent and the target's work does not come back to the caller as a tool result. The module docstring says "in handoff the agents themselves decide who to handoff to next by invoking a tool call that names the target agent" and "The entire conversation is maintained and reused on every hop" (`_handoff.py:16-24`).

Semantics. The call does not wait for the task. A completed task returns the subagent's raw text or "(no output)", a failed one returns "Task failed: {task_info.error_text or 'Unknown error'}", a lost one returns "Task state was lost (reference unavailable).", a running one returns "Task {task_id} is still running.", and an unknown id returns "Error: No task found with ID {task_id}." (`_background_agents.py:583-597`). Each call first refreshes task state, so a task that finished since the last check shows as completed or failed (`_background_agents.py:235-260`). A task is marked `lost` when its in-flight reference is gone, which the source says happens when the provider instance is lost, for example across a process restart (`_background_agents.py:246-250`, `:341-345`).

The description is the function's raw docstring (`_tools.py:1745`), which spans three source lines and is shown here without its code indentation.

Description (verbatim, .NET):

```text
Wait until the first of the specified background tasks completes or the configured timeout expires. Provide one or more task IDs. Returns a status message containing the ID of the task that completed first. On timeout, the tasks remain running and this tool can be called again to continue waiting.
```

Parameters (.NET lambda signature, verbatim):

```csharp
            AIFunctionFactory.Create(
                async (List<int> taskIds, CancellationToken cancellationToken) =>
```

Source (description and parameters): Microsoft Agent Framework source at commit fd52de7, `dotnet/src/Microsoft.Agents.AI/Harness/BackgroundAgents/BackgroundAgentsProvider.cs:669-670` and `:746-751` - source at commit, 2026-10-09 (fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog).

Semantics. The call blocks until the first listed running task finishes or the timeout expires; the timeout is set by the developer, not the model: Python `wait_timeout_seconds` defaults to 300 seconds (`_background_agents.py:30`, `:296-334`), and .NET `WaitTimeout` defaults to five minutes with a maximum of 4,294,967,294 milliseconds (`BackgroundAgentsProviderOptions.cs:16-17`, `:43-51`). It returns only the id and status, "Task {completed_id} finished with status: {status_str}.", so the model must call `background_agents_get_task_results` to read the output (`_background_agents.py:560-578`); Python statuses are `running`, `completed`, `failed`, and `lost` (`:47-53`), and .NET prints the enum names `Running`, `Completed`, `Failed`, and `Lost` (`BackgroundTaskStatus.cs:12-34`, `BackgroundAgentsProvider.cs:743`). On timeout it returns "No background task completed within {self._wait_timeout_seconds} seconds. The tasks are still running; call this tool again if you wish to continue waiting." and leaves the tasks running (`_background_agents.py:554-558`). If none of the ids is running it returns "Task {already_complete.id} is not running; current status: {already_complete.status.value}." for a finished task or "Error: None of the specified task IDs correspond to running tasks.", and an empty list returns "Error: No task IDs provided." (`_background_agents.py:526-546`). The timeout was added on 2026-08-27 in PR #7908 (forum or issue, merged 2026-08-27).

The README at this commit says "AutoGen is now in maintenance mode. It will not receive new features or enhancements and is community managed going forward." and calls Microsoft Agent Framework "the enterprise-ready successor to AutoGen". The model sees one handoff tool per configured target, `transfer_to_<target>`, and one tool per agent wrapped with `AgentTool`. There is no background, status, or cancel tool.

#### `<agent_name>` (spawn)

Description (verbatim, generated):

```text
{agent.description}
```

Source: AutoGen source at commit 027ecf0, `python/packages/autogen-agentchat/src/autogen_agentchat/tools/_agent.py:79-83`, which passes `agent.name` and `agent.description` as the tool name and description; AutoGen adds no text of its own - source at commit, 2026-04-06 (fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog).

Parameters (Python pydantic model from source at commit 027ecf0, verbatim):

```python
class TaskRunnerToolArgs(BaseModel):
    """Input for the TaskRunnerTool."""

    task: Annotated[str, "The task to be executed."]
```

Source: AutoGen source at commit 027ecf0, `python/packages/autogen-agentchat/src/autogen_agentchat/tools/_task_runner_tool.py:14-17` - source at commit, 2026-04-06 (fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog). The tool is built with `strict=True` (`_task_runner_tool.py:34-40`), and autogen-core sends the `properties` and `required` lists from `model_json_schema()` as the parameters (`autogen-core/src/autogen_core/tools/_base.py:114-148`). Whether the bare-string `Annotated` metadata reaches the JSON Schema as a `description` is not in the sources.

Semantics. `AgentTool(agent)` names the tool after the wrapped agent's `name` and uses its `description`, so the parameter model shown is what AutoGen generates for each wrapped agent (`_agent.py:79-83`). The call is blocking: `run` awaits `self._task_runner.run(task=args.task, ...)` and returns a `TaskResult`, which reaches the model through `return_value_as_string` as every non-user message joined as "{source}: {text}" with blank lines between them, or only the last message when `return_value_as_last_message=True` (`_task_runner_tool.py:42-66`). The docstring says "When using AgentTool, you **must** disable parallel tool calls in the model client configuration to avoid concurrency issues. Agents cannot run concurrently as they maintain internal state that would conflict with parallel execution." (`_agent.py:25-30`). A sibling `TeamTool` wraps a whole team with the same `task` argument model, and its name and description are supplied by the developer (`tools/_team.py:112-116`).

#### `transfer_to_<target>` (handoff)

Description (verbatim):

```text
Handoff to {target}.
```

Source: AutoGen source at commit 027ecf0, `python/packages/autogen-agentchat/src/autogen_agentchat/base/_handoff.py:33-34`, the default `f"Handoff to {values['target']}."` used when the `Handoff` has no `description`; `{target}` is the target agent's name - source at commit, 2026-04-06 (fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog).

Parameters (Python function from source at commit 027ecf0, verbatim):

```python
        def _handoff_tool() -> str:
            return self.message

        return FunctionTool(_handoff_tool, name=self.name, description=self.description, strict=True)
```

Source: AutoGen source at commit 027ecf0, `python/packages/autogen-agentchat/src/autogen_agentchat/base/_handoff.py:54-57` - source at commit, 2026-04-06 (fetched 2026-10-10 for this catalog). The function takes no arguments; the JSON Schema text autogen-core generates for it is not in the sources.

Semantics. The default name is `f"transfer_to_{values['target']}".lower()`, so the target name is lowercased, and a custom `name` must be a valid Python identifier (`_handoff.py:35-43`); a handoff given as a plain string is the target agent's name (`_assistant_agent.py:200-203`). The tool returns the handoff message, by default "Transferred to {target}, adopting the role of {target} immediately." (`_handoff.py:44-47`), and `AssistantAgent` then ends its turn with a `HandoffMessage` whose content is that message, whose target is the handoff target, and whose context holds any other tool calls and results from the same turn (`_assistant_agent.py:1347-1405`). Control moves to the other agent and does not come back to the caller as a tool result: "The transfer is only executed when the team is in :class:`~autogen_agentchat.teams.Swarm`." (`_assistant_agent.py:200-202`), and the `Swarm` manager makes the target of the latest `HandoffMessage` the next speaker (`_swarm_group_chat.py:82-98`). If the model makes several handoff calls in one turn, only the first runs, with the warning "Multiple handoffs detected. Only the first is executed: ..." (`_assistant_agent.py:1350-1362`).
